Chapter 9: Distributed Transactions

9.1 Introduction and Motivation

A transaction is a unit of work that satisfies the ACID properties: Atomicity (all operations happen or none do), Consistency (the system moves from one valid state to another), Isolation (concurrent transactions do not observe intermediate states), and Durability (committed effects survive crashes). In a single-node database, these properties are implemented with well-understood machinery: write-ahead logs (WALs), lock tables or multiversion concurrency control (MVCC), and careful buffer management. When the state involved in a transaction spans multiple processes, machines, or independent services, the guarantees must be constructed out of network messages, local logs, and coordination protocols. This chapter is about that construction.

The central difficulty is the network itself. A distributed system cannot distinguish between the following situations:

The participant crashed before receiving the message.

The participant crashed after receiving the message but before replying.

The message is delayed in the network.

The reply is delayed.

The participant is slow, but alive.

Any protocol that must reach a decision — commit or abort — in the presence of these ambiguities is called a commit protocol. We will see that the design space of commit protocols is governed by a fundamental tension: the desire to make progress (availability) versus the desire to never make an unsafe decision (safety). The FLP impossibility result [1] proves that in an asynchronous network with even one possible crash, no deterministic protocol can guarantee both termination and agreement. Practical protocols therefore either block (wait indefinitely for a failed participant), or add assumptions (failure detectors, timeouts) that allow them to make progress at the cost of occasionally making a "wrong" guess about a participant's state.

9.1.1 The Two Generals Problem

Before examining commit protocols, consider the simplest formulation of the problem. Two generals, on opposite sides of a valley, must agree on a time to attack. Their only communication is via messengers who may be captured. Each general requires certainty that the other knows the plan before committing. But any acknowledgment of the plan itself requires an acknowledgment, leading to an infinite regress. There is no finite protocol that gives both generals absolute certainty. The best they can do is agree on a protocol that gives probabilistic certainty, or accept a protocol where one side unilaterally decides after a timeout.

The Two Generals problem is the distributed analogue of the commit decision: the "commit" message from a coordinator to a participant, and the participant's "ack," cannot be delivered with certainty. Any commit protocol must handle the case where the coordinator believes the participant has committed but the participant never received the instruction.

9.1.2 The Blocking Problem

A commit protocol is blocking if, after a failure, some correct participants cannot make progress (cannot decide commit or abort) until the failed participant recovers. Blocking is undesirable because a single crashed node can hold locks and resources across the entire system indefinitely. Non-blocking protocols exist but require stronger assumptions or more message rounds. We will examine this tradeoff in detail.

9.2 Two-Phase Commit (2PC)

Two-phase commit is the canonical atomic commit protocol. It was described by Gray [2] and formalized by Lampson and Schmidt. It is used in XA transactions, distributed SQL databases (e.g., older versions of PostgreSQL with foreign data wrappers, Spanner's commit protocol), and many transaction managers.

Coordinator: the process that initiates the commit protocol. It may be the node that received the client's request, or a separate transaction manager.

This is called "lock coupling" or "distributed two-phase locking." The duration of lock holding is extended by the commit protocol's message rounds, which can reduce concurrency.

9.4 Paxos Commit

Paxos Commit, described by Gray and Lamport [4], uses the Paxos consensus algorithm to implement atomic commit. The key idea is to replace the coordinator (a single point of failure) with a consensus group that decides the outcome.

9.4.1 Consensus Background

Paxos solves the problem of getting a set of processes to agree on a single value, even in the presence of crashes, under the asynchronous network model with a failure detector (or timeouts). It guarantees:

Agreement: No two correct processes decide differently.

Validity: The decided value was proposed by some process.

Termination: Eventually, a value is decided (assuming a majority of processes are alive).

Paxos operates with two roles: proposers (or leaders) and acceptors. Acceptors maintain state (promised ballot number, accepted value). A leader proposes a value by running a two-phase protocol: Phase 1 prepares (promises not to accept earlier ballots), Phase 2 accepts.

9.4.2 Paxos Commit Protocol

In Paxos Commit, each participant of the transaction runs its own Paxos instance to decide its vote. The global outcome is the conjunction of all votes: commit if and only if every participant's Paxos instance decides "yes."

The protocol:

Each participant Pi runs a Paxos instance Vi to decide its vote (yes or no).

The coordinator (or any process) acts as the leader for all instances.

To commit, the leader must ensure that all instances decide "yes."

If any instance decides "no," the leader ensures all instances decide "no" (or the ones that decided "yes" are overridden to "no" — but Paxos does not allow overriding a decided value, so instead the leader ensures that no instance decides "yes" until all are known to be able to).

The subtlety is that Paxos instances decide independently. To ensure atomicity, the leader must not allow any instance to decide "yes" until it is certain that all instances will decide "yes." This is achieved by running the Paxos instances in a coordinated way: the leader first runs Phase 1 (prepare) on all instances. If all succeed, the leader knows that all participants are prepared. Then the leader runs Phase 2 (accept "yes") on all instances. If any participant fails during Phase 2, the leader runs Phase 2 (accept "no") on all instances that have not yet decided.

The key property is that a participant that has accepted "yes" in Phase 2 but not yet decided cannot unilaterally abort — it must wait for the leader's decision, just as in 2PC. However, if the leader crashes, a new leader can be elected and can complete the protocol, because Paxos guarantees that a majority of acceptors can make progress.

9.4.3 Paxos Commit vs. 2PC

The critical difference is that 2PC has a single coordinator whose failure blocks the protocol. Paxos Commit replaces the coordinator with a group of acceptors. As long as a majority of acceptors are alive, the protocol can make progress. The cost is that Paxos requires more messages and more state (each acceptor must maintain per-instance state).

In practice, Paxos Commit is rarely implemented as described. Instead, systems like Spanner use Paxos (or Raft) to replicate the coordinator's state, and then run 2PC between the replicated coordinators. This gives the fault tolerance of consensus with the simplicity of 2PC.

function paxos_commit(txn):
    # Phase 1: Prepare on all instances
    for each participant Pi:
        prepare_result = run_paxos_phase1(Vi, ballot)
        if prepare_result is FAILURE:
            # Some instance cannot be prepared; abort
            for each participant Pj:
                run_paxos_phase2(Vj, ABORT)
            return ABORT

    # Phase 2: Accept on all instances
    all_prepared = true
    for each participant Pi:
        accept_result = run_paxos_phase2(Vi, COMMIT)
        if accept_result is FAILURE:

        return ABORT

    return COMMIT
```

9.5 Saga-Based Compensation

When the transaction spans independent services that cannot participate in a distributed transaction protocol (e.g., microservices with separate databases), the standard approach is to model the transaction as a sequence of local transactions, each with a compensating action. This is the saga pattern, originally described by Garcia-Molina and Salem [5] for long-lived transactions.

9.5.1 Saga Execution

A saga is a sequence of local transactions T1, T2, ..., Tn. Each Ti has a compensating transaction Ci. The saga executes Ti in order. If all complete, the saga is committed. If some Tj fails, the saga executes the compensations Cj-1, Cj-2, ..., C1 in reverse order.

The compensations must be semantically undoable: executing Ti followed by Ci leaves the system in a state equivalent to not having executed Ti. However, the compensation is not a true undo — it is a new transaction that semantically reverses the effect. For example, if Ti is "charge credit card $100," the compensation Ci is "refund credit card $100." The refund is a new charge (negative), not a deletion of the original charge.

9.5.2 Worked Example: Banking Transfer as a Saga

The transfer from Account A (Service S1) to Account B (Service S2) can be modeled as a saga:

T1 (S1): Debit Account A by $100. Compensation C1: Credit Account A by $100.

T2 (S2): Credit Account B by $100. Compensation C2: Debit Account B by $100 (if possible; if the account has been closed, C2 might be a no-op or an alert).

Execution:

```
Orchestrator          S1 (Account A)         S2 (Account B)
     |                     |                      |
     |--T1: debit A------->|                      |
     |                     | (balance: 500→400)   |
     |<--T1 ok-------------|                      |
     |                     |                      |
     |--T2: credit B----------------------------->|
     |                     |                      | (balance: 300→400)
     |<--T2 ok------------------------------------|
     |                     |                      |
     | (saga committed)    |                      |
```

Failure at T2:

```
Orchestrator          S1 (Account A)         S2 (Account B)
     |                     |                      |
     |--T1: debit A------->|                      |
     |<--T1 ok-------------|                      |
     |                     |                      |
     |--T2: credit B----------------------------->|
     |<--T2 FAIL (timeout)-|                      |
     |                     |                      |
     |--C1: credit A------>|                      |
     |                     | (balance: 400→500)   |
     |<--C1 ok-------------|                      |
     |                     |                      |
     | (saga aborted)      |                      |
```

9.5.3 Saga Orchestration vs. Choreography

There are two styles of saga coordination:

Orchestration: A central orchestrator (a state machine) drives the saga. It sends commands to services and tracks the state. This is explicit and easy to reason about, but the orchestrator is a potential single point of failure (though it can be replicated).

Choreography: Services react to events. There is no central coordinator. Each service knows what to do next based on the outcome of its own transaction and the events it observes. This is more loosely coupled but harder to reason about — the flow is implicit in the event handlers.

9.5.4 Isolation in Sagas

Sagas do not provide isolation. Because each local transaction commits immediately, other transactions can observe intermediate states. In the banking example, after T1 (debit A) but before T2 (credit B), the total balance across A and B is $100 short. Another transaction that reads both balances would see an inconsistent state.

This is called the anomaly of lost updates or dirty reads (depending on the isolation level). Mitigations include:

Semantic locks: The service that executed T1 places a "saga lock" on Account A, preventing other sagas from using A until the saga completes. This is application-level locking.

Compensating transactions: Instead of preventing anomalies, design compensations that handle them. For example, if another transaction credited Account A between T1 and C1, the compensation C1 must not blindly add $100 — it must check the current balance and adjust.

Commutative operations: Design operations so that they commute (order doesn't matter). For example, debits and credits commute if they are on different accounts. If they are on the same account, they commute if the balance never goes negative.

9.5.5 Saga Pseudocode

```
class Saga:
    def __init__(self):
        self.steps = []  # list of (execute_fn, compensate_fn)
        self.completed = []

    def add_step(self, execute_fn, compensate_fn):
        self.steps.append((execute_fn, compensate_fn))

    def execute(self):
        for i, (execute_fn, compensate_fn) in enumerate(self.steps):
            try:
                execute_fn()
                self.completed.append(i)
            except Exception as e:
                # Compensation phase
                for j in reversed(self.completed):
                    compensate_fn = self.steps[j][1]
                    try:
                        compensate_fn()
                    except Exception as ce:
                        log_error(f"Compensation {j} failed: {ce}")
                        # May require manual intervention
                raise SagaAborted(f"Step {i} failed: {e}") from e
        return SagaCommitted()
```

9.5.6 Handling Compensation Failures

If a compensation fails (e.g., the service is down), the saga cannot be rolled back cleanly. The orchestrator must retry the compensation. If retries are exhausted, the saga enters a "compensation failed" state that requires manual intervention (e.g., an operations dashboard). This is a fundamental limitation: sagas trade atomicity for availability, and the residual inconsistency must be handled by humans or by additional automation.

9.6 Transactional Outbox Pattern

When a service commits a local transaction and then publishes a message (e.g., to a message broker), there is a race: the service might crash after committing but before publishing, or the publish might fail. The transactional outbox pattern solves this by writing the message to a database table (the "outbox") in the same local transaction as the state change. A separate process (the "relay" or "poller") reads the outbox and publishes the messages.

9.6.1 The Problem

Consider a service that debits an account and then sends an event "AccountDebited" to a message broker:

```
function debit_account(account_id, amount):
    db.begin()
    db.execute("UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - ? WHERE id = ?", amount, account_id)
    db.commit()
    # If the service crashes here, the event is never sent
    broker.publish("AccountDebited", {account_id, amount})
```

If the crash happens after commit but before publish, downstream services never learn about the debit. If the publish happens before the commit, and the commit fails, downstream services see an event for a debit that never happened.

9.6.2 The Solution

Write the event to an outbox table in the same transaction:

```
function debit_account(account_id, amount):
    db.begin()
    db.execute("UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - ? WHERE id = ?", amount, account_id)
    db.execute("INSERT INTO outbox (id, topic, payload) VALUES (?, ?, ?)",
               uuid4(), "AccountDebited", json({account_id, amount}))
    db.commit()
```

A relay process polls the outbox and publishes messages:

```

9.6.3 Exactly-Once Delivery Semantics

The outbox pattern provides at-least-once delivery: if the relay crashes after publishing but before deleting the message from the outbox, the message will be published again when the relay restarts. Exactly-once delivery is impossible to achieve in a general distributed system (the Two Generals problem again): the relay cannot atomically "publish and mark as published" across two independent systems (the broker and the database).

However, exactly-once processing can be achieved by making the consumer idempotent. The consumer tracks the messages it has processed (e.g., by message ID) and ignores duplicates. Alternatively, the consumer's state update can be made idempotent (e.g., "set balance = balance - 100" is not idempotent, but "set balance = 400 where version = 5" is).

In the outbox pattern, the relay can use the database transaction to atomically mark messages as "publishing" and then "published," reducing (but not eliminating) duplicates. Some systems use a "claim" table with a lease to ensure only one relay processes a message at a time.

9.6.4 Outbox and Message Ordering

The outbox pattern naturally provides per-partition ordering if the relay publishes messages in the order they appear in the outbox (e.g., ordered by a sequence number). However, if multiple relay instances poll the same outbox, ordering can be violated. Solutions include:

Single relay: Only one relay instance polls the outbox (a single point of failure, but simple).

Partitioned relay: Multiple relays, each responsible for a subset of messages (e.g., partitioned by account ID). Messages within a partition are ordered; across partitions, ordering is not guaranteed.

Sequence numbers: The consumer tracks the last-seen sequence number per producer and buffers out-of-order messages.

9.6.5 Outbox and the Banking Transfer

In the saga-based banking transfer, the outbox pattern ensures that the orchestrator's commands are reliably delivered to the services:

Service S1 (Account A) executes T1 (debit) and writes an event "DebitCompleted" to its outbox.

The relay publishes "DebitCompleted" to the message broker.

The orchestrator consumes "DebitCompleted" and sends T2 (credit) to Service S2.

Service S2 executes T2 and writes "CreditCompleted" to its outbox.

The relay publishes "CreditCompleted."

The orchestrator consumes "CreditCompleted" and completes the saga.

If S1's relay crashes after publishing but before deleting from the outbox, the message is published twice. The orchestrator must be idempotent: it tracks the saga ID and step, and ignores duplicate completions.

9.7 Exactly-Once Semantics: A Deeper Look

The phrase "exactly-once delivery" is often used loosely. It is important to distinguish:

Exactly-once delivery: The message is delivered to the consumer exactly once. This is impossible in a general distributed system (the consumer cannot distinguish a duplicate from a retry).

Exactly-once effect (or exactly-once processing): The message's effect on the consumer's state is applied exactly once. This is achievable if the consumer is idempotent or if it tracks processed messages.

Exactly-once transaction: The producer's state change and the message publication are atomic. This is what the outbox pattern achieves (at the producer side).

The combination of the outbox pattern (atomic write of state + message) and idempotent consumers (deduplication by message ID) gives the appearance of exactly-once semantics end-to-end, even though the underlying delivery is at-least-once.

A distributed transaction is a transaction whose effects span more than one node. The moment a transaction touches two machines, the fundamental problem of distributed commit arises: the machines must agree, despite partial failures, whether the transaction committed or aborted. This chapter treats that problem with the rigor it deserves. We begin with the two-phase commit protocol and its variants, prove its correctness properties, and expose its blocking behavior. We then study three-phase commit, which eliminates blocking under a restricted failure model, and Paxos Commit, which eliminates blocking under asynchronous crash failures. Finally, we examine saga-based compensation, which sidesteps atomic commit entirely by restructuring applications around compensating actions.

Throughout, we assume a system of N processes {p₁, p₂, ..., p_N}, each managing a set of objects. Processes communicate via reliable message passing over eventually-fair channels: if p sends a message to q and both remain operational, q eventually receives it. A process is operational if it executes its protocol correctly; a process crashes if it halts permanently or temporarily stops taking steps. We do not assume Byzantine behavior in this chapter.

12.1 The Atomic Commitment Problem

Definition 12.1 (Atomic Commitment). An atomic commitment protocol (ACP) is a protocol in which each process pᵢ, given a transaction T, decides one of two values: commit or abort. The protocol must satisfy:

AC1 (Agreement): No two processes decide differently.

AC2 (Validity): If any process decides commit, then every process voted yes.

AC3 (Termination): Every correct process eventually decides.

AC4 (Non-triviality): If there are no failures and every process votes yes, then the decision is commit.

The validity condition AC2 encodes the semantics of local locks and local recovery: a process votes yes only if it is prepared to commit its local portion of the transaction, meaning it has written redo records to stable storage and released nothing yet. A process votes no if it detected a local constraint violation, ran out of disk space, or simply chose to abort.

The non-triviality condition AC4 prevents the trivial protocol that always aborts. Together, AC2 and AC4 imply that when all processes vote yes and no failures occur, commit is the outcome.

Theorem 12.1 (Impossibility of Non-blocking ACP with Unilateral Abort). No atomic commitment protocol can simultaneously satisfy AC1–AC4 and guarantee that a correct process decides in bounded time if any process may crash after voting yes but before deciding.

Proof. Suppose such a protocol exists. Consider an execution σ in which all processes vote yes, all are correct, and the protocol reaches a state S from which commit is inevitable (i.e., every extension of σ from S results in commit). Such a state must exist by AC4 and termination: in the failure-free execution, the protocol must eventually reach a point where the decision is fixed.

Now consider a second execution σ' identical to σ up to state S, but in which process p₁ crashes immediately after entering S. By assumption, the remaining processes must decide in bounded time. They cannot decide commit, because p₁ might have crashed before sending some message that would have caused another process to vote no — wait, all voted yes. Let us refine: they cannot decide commit, because in a third execution σ'' identical to σ' up to S, process p₁ crashes before writing its prepare record to stable storage, and upon recovery, p₁'s transaction is lost, forcing p₁ to abort. If the others decided commit, AC1 is violated in σ''.

They also cannot decide abort, because in σ' itself, p₁ is correct (it merely crashed in σ'), and by termination p₁ must eventually decide; but p₁, having voted yes and received no contrary information, may decide commit, violating AC1.

Since any decision violates some requirement, no such protocol exists. ∎

The reader should note the crux: the decision commit is irrevocable, but a crashed process's vote may be indistinguishable from a crashed process's abort. This ambiguity is the fundamental obstacle. Two-phase commit accepts blocking as the price of safety. Three-phase commit removes the ambiguity by adding a pre-commit state. Paxos Commit removes it by making the vote itself replicated.

12.2 Two-Phase Commit

12.2.1 Protocol Description

Two-phase commit (2PC) [Gray 1978; Lampson and Sturgis 1976] involves a coordinator and participants. The coordinator may be one of the participants or a separate process. We describe the protocol from the coordinator's perspective, then prove its properties.

Phase 1 (Voting):

The coordinator sends a PREPARE message to every participant.

Each participant pᵢ executes the transaction's local portion up to the point where all locks are held. If pᵢ is willing to commit, it writes a prepare record (containing all redo and undo information) to its stable log, then replies YES. If pᵢ is unwilling, it writes an abort record and replies NO.

Phase 2 (Decision):

If the coordinator receives YES from all participants, it writes a commit record to its own log and sends COMMIT to every participant. Otherwise, it writes an abort record and sends ABORT.

Each participant that receives COMMIT writes a commit record to its log and releases locks. Each participant that receives ABORT writes an abort record and releases locks.

The prepare record is the participant's promise: once pᵢ writes it and replies YES, pᵢ has ceded the decision to the coordinator. pᵢ must remain prepared to commit or abort indefinitely until it receives the coordinator's decision. This is the source of blocking.

12.2.2 Pseudocode

We present the protocol in a Go-like pseudocode for clarity.

```go
// Coordinator state
type CoordinatorState int

const (
    Init CoordinatorState = iota
    Waiting          // Sent PREPARE, collecting votes
    Decided          // Sent decision
)

func (c *Coordinator) Run(txn *Transaction) Decision {
    c.state = Waiting
    votes := make(map[ProcessID]bool)

    for _, p := range c.participants {
        go func(p ProcessID) {
            reply := c.sendPrepare(p, txn)
            c.mu.Lock()
            votes[p] = reply
            c.mu.Unlock()
        }(p)
    }

    // Wait for all votes or timeout
    for len(votes) < len(c.participants) {
        if c.timedOut() {
            break
        }
        time.Sleep(pollInterval)
    }

    decision := Commit
    for _, v := range votes {
        if !v {
            decision = Abort
            break
        }
    }

    // Coordinator writes decision record to its own stable log
    c.writeLog(decision)

    c.state = Decided
    for _, p := range c.participants {
        c.sendDecision(p, decision)
    }
    return decision
}
```

```go
// Participant state
type ParticipantState int

const (
    Working ParticipantState = iota
    Prepared
    Committed
    Aborted
)

func (p *Participant) OnPrepare(txn *Transaction) Vote {
    if !p.canCommit(txn) {
        p.writeAbortRecord(txn)
        p.state = Aborted
        return No
    }
    // Write prepare record: flush redo/undo to stable storage
    p.writePrepareRecord(txn)
    p.state = Prepared
    return Yes
}

func (p *Participant) OnDecision(d Decision) {
    switch p.state {
    case Prepared:
        if d == Commit {
            p.writeCommitRecord(txn)
            p.state = Committed
        } else {
            p.writeAbortRecord(txn)
            p.state = Aborted
        }
        p.releaseLocks(txn)
    case Committed, Aborted:
        // Already decided; idempotent
    default:
        // Unexpected: vote was No, or decision arrived before prepare
    }
}
```

12.2.3 Correctness

Theorem 12.2 (2PC Satisfies AC1–AC4). In any execution of 2PC in which no more than the assumed failures occur, the protocol satisfies agreement, validity, termination for correct processes, and non-triviality.

Proof sketch.

AC4: With no failures and yes votes, the coordinator receives all yes votes, writes commit, and sends commit. Participants commit.

AC2: A participant votes yes only after writing its prepare record; the coordinator sends commit only if all votes are yes. If any participant votes no, the coordinator aborts.

AC1: The coordinator decides a single value and communicates it. Participants decide only after receiving the coordinator's decision (or after a recovery procedure that we discuss in §12.4). Since the coordinator's decision is written to stable storage before being sent, and participants' decisions are derived from it, agreement holds.

AC3: Correct participants eventually receive the coordinator's decision, assuming the coordinator is correct and channels are reliable. ∎

Theorem 12.3 (2PC Blocking). If the coordinator crashes after sending PREPARE but before sending its decision, and participant pᵢ has voted yes while participant pⱼ has not yet voted, then pᵢ cannot decide until the coordinator recovers.

Proof. pᵢ has voted yes and is in state Prepared. pᵢ cannot unilaterally commit: the coordinator might have received a no from pⱼ (or from a participant not yet heard from) and decided abort. pᵢ cannot unilaterally abort: the coordinator might have received yes from all and decided commit. Since pᵢ cannot distinguish these cases, and since deciding incorrectly violates AC1, pᵢ must wait. ∎

This blocking is not a corner case; it is the normal consequence of a coordinator crash at the wrong moment. In practice, 2PC implementations mitigate blocking with:

Cooperative termination: a blocked participant pᵢ queries other participants. If pⱼ has decided, pⱼ shares its decision. If all queried participants are in Prepared, pᵢ may infer abort (since the coordinator cannot have committed without all yes votes — but this inference is only valid if no participant is still in Working; see Exercise 12.3).

Coordinator log inspection: upon coordinator recovery, participants read the coordinator's stable log to determine the decision.

Timeout-based abort: a participant in Working that times out waiting for the coordinator's decision aborts unilaterally. This is safe because a Working participant has not yet promised anything; the coordinator cannot have committed without this participant's yes vote.

12.2.4 Variants

Presumed Abort (2PC-PA) [Skeen 1981; Mohan, Lindsay, and Obermarck 1986]. The coordinator's abort decision requires no log record: if the coordinator's log contains no record for transaction T, the presumed outcome is abort. Participants that vote no need not log their abort. The coordinator need not log the abort decision; it suffices to log the commit decision. This reduces the number of forced log writes for read-only transactions to zero.

Presumed Commit (2PC-PC). The dual: absence of a log record implies commit. This is advantageous when most transactions commit, but requires the coordinator to log the transaction's identity before sending PREPARE, adding a forced write in the common case. Presumed commit is rarely used in practice because the presumed-abort optimization captures most of the benefit without the extra write.

Read-only optimization. A participant that performs no writes may vote "read-only" and immediately forget the transaction. The coordinator excludes read-only participants from the commit decision. This eliminates the prepare record and the decision wait for such participants.

Consensus commit [Gray and Lamport 2004]. Reformulates 2PC as an instance of Paxos per participant, integrating replication with commit. We defer discussion to §12.5.

12.3 Three-Phase Commit

Three-phase commit (3PC) [Skeen 1981] augments 2PC with an intermediate pre-commit phase to eliminate blocking under crash failures (but not under network partitions).

12.3.1 Protocol Description

Phase 1 (Can-Commit): The coordinator sends a CAN-COMMIT message. Each participant votes YES or NO as in 2PC.

Phase 2 (Pre-Commit): If all votes are YES, the coordinator sends PRE-COMMIT. Each participant that receives PRE-COMMIT writes a prepare record and acknowledges. If any vote is NO, the coordinator sends ABORT.

Phase 3 (Do-Commit): After receiving acknowledgments from all participants, the coordinator sends DO-COMMIT. Each participant commits.

The key insight: the pre-commit state is a "safe" state from which abort is impossible. A participant in pre-commit knows that all participants voted yes. Therefore, a participant in pre-commit that times out may unilaterally commit, knowing that no other participant can be in a state where abort is still possible.

12.3.2 Timeout Rules

3PC's non-blocking property depends on specific timeout behavior:

A participant in Working that times out aborts (as in 2PC).

A participant in Pre-Commit that times out commits.

A participant that receives ABORT in any state aborts.

A participant that receives DO-COMMIT commits.

Theorem 12.4 (3PC Non-blocking under Crash Failures). In a system with crash failures but no network partitions, 3PC satisfies AC1–AC4 and guarantees that every correct participant decides within bounded time, even if the coordinator crashes.

Proof sketch. Consider any correct participant pᵢ after the coordinator crashes. pᵢ is in one of three states:

Working: pᵢ has not voted yes. pᵢ aborts on timeout. No other correct participant can commit, because the coordinator requires all yes votes to enter pre-commit, and pᵢ's yes vote is a prerequisite. Since pᵢ is correct and has not voted yes, the coordinator (if correct) could not have sent pre-commit to all participants.

Pre-Commit: pᵢ commits on timeout. No other correct participant can abort, because pᵢ's pre-commit state implies the coordinator sent pre-commit, which implies all participants voted yes. A participant in Working cannot abort "safely" without risking disagreement — but a participant in Working that times out aborts only if it has not voted yes. Since all participants voted yes (implied by pre-commit), no participant is in Working with a no vote. A participant in Pre-Commit that times out commits; a participant in Working that times out aborts — but these cannot coexist, because pre-commit implies all yes votes, and all yes votes imply no participant is in Working with a no vote.

Committed or Aborted: pᵢ has already decided.

The critical invariant is: no execution reaches a state where one participant is in Pre-Commit (or beyond) while another is in Working (or has aborted). This invariant holds because the coordinator sends pre-commit only after receiving all yes votes, and a participant enters Working only before voting. ∎

Theorem 12.5 (3PC Blocking under Network Partitions). If the network partitions, 3PC may violate agreement.

Proof. Suppose the coordinator sends PRE-COMMIT to participants p₁, p₂ and crashes before sending DO-COMMIT. Suppose the network partitions p₁ from p₂. p₁ receives PRE-COMMIT and enters Pre-Commit. p₂ does not receive PRE-COMMIT and remains in Working. p₂ times out and aborts. p₁ times out and commits. Agreement is violated. ∎

Because of this vulnerability, 3PC is rarely used in practice. The additional round of communication increases latency, and the protocol's safety depends on the absence of partitions — an assumption that is difficult to guarantee in real networks.

12.3.3 Worked Example

Consider three participants A, B, C coordinating a transfer of $100 from A's account to C's account.

Happy path:

Coordinator → A, B, C: CAN-COMMIT.

A, B, C → Coordinator: YES.

Coordinator → A, B, C: PRE-COMMIT.

A, B, C → Coordinator: ACK.

Coordinator → A, B, C: DO-COMMIT.

A, B, C: commit, release locks.

Failure path (coordinator crashes after PRE-COMMIT):

Steps 1–4 complete. Coordinator crashes before step 5.

A, B, C are in Pre-Commit. Each times out and commits independently.

Agreement holds: all commit.

Failure path (coordinator crashes before PRE-COMMIT):

Steps 1–2 complete. Coordinator crashes.

A, B, C are in Working. Each times out and aborts.

Agreement holds: all abort.

Failure path (partition):

Steps 1–2 complete. Coordinator sends PRE-COMMIT to A only, crashes. Network partitions A from B.

A: Pre-Commit → commits on timeout.

B: Working → aborts on timeout.

Agreement violated.

12.4 Failure Recovery

Recovery is the discipline by which a crashed process resumes operation without violating the atomic commitment guarantees. Recovery is not an afterthought; it is the mechanism that resolves the ambiguity identified in Theorem 12.1.

12.4.1 Write-Ahead Logging

Every participant maintains a stable log. The log is a sequence of records, each containing a transaction identifier, a record type, and payload. The write-ahead logging (WAL) protocol imposes two rules:

Rule 1 (redo): The redo records for a transaction's updates must be on stable storage before the updates are applied to the database (or before the transaction commits).

Rule 2 (undo): The undo records for a transaction's updates must be on stable storage before the updates are applied to the database.

In 2PC, the prepare record serves both roles: it contains redo information (so the transaction can be completed after recovery) and undo information (so it can be rolled back). The prepare record must be forced to stable storage before the participant votes yes.

12.4.2 Recovery Procedure

When participant pᵢ recovers from a crash, it scans its log for transactions that were in flight. For each such transaction T:

If the log contains a commit record for T: redo T's updates and complete the commit. pᵢ may need to inform the coordinator (if pᵢ is also the coordinator) or simply release locks.

If the log contains an abort record for T: undo T's updates and complete the abort.

If the log contains a prepare record for T but no decision record: pᵢ is in Prepared. pᵢ must determine the global outcome. It may:

Query the coordinator. If the coordinator is operational, it responds with the decision.

Query other participants. If any has decided, that participant shares the decision (cooperative termination).

If the coordinator is unreachable and no participant has decided, pᵢ remains blocked (in 2PC) or applies the timeout rule (in 3PC: commit if in Pre-Commit, abort if in Working).

If the log contains no record for T: pᵢ never voted yes. pᵢ aborts unilaterally.

If pᵢ is the coordinator and its log contains a commit record for T, pᵢ broadcasts commit. If its log contains an abort record, pᵢ broadcasts abort. If its log contains a prepare record but no decision, pᵢ (as coordinator) has not decided; it may re-run the voting phase.

12.4.3 Idempotence and Re transmission

All decision messages must be idempotent: receiving COMMIT twice must have the same effect as receiving it once. This is trivially satisfied by the participant's state machine: once in Committed, a second COMMIT is a no-op. Similarly, PREPARE retransmission after a participant crash is handled by the participant's log: if the prepare record exists, the participant re-sends YES without re-executing the transaction.

12.4.4 Three-Generation Logging [Lomet 1977]

Lomet's three-generation scheme organizes log records into generations to bound the amount of log that must be scanned at recovery. Generation g contains records for transactions active during interval I_g. At recovery, only the current generation and the immediately preceding generation need be examined. Checkpoint records delimit generations. The scheme reduces recovery time from O(total log) to O(log since last checkpoint).

12.5 Paxos Commit

Paxos Commit [Gray and Lamport 2004] replaces the single coordinator with a replicated consensus group per participant. The result is an atomic commitment protocol that is non-blocking under asynchronous crash failures (with a majority of each consensus group operational), satisfying AC1–AC3 without the blocking of 2PC.

12.5.1 Architecture

For each participant pᵢ, there is a consensus group Pᵢ of 2fᵢ + 1 processes. Each group Pᵢ runs an instance of Paxos to decide pᵢ's vote: 1 (yes) or 0 (no). The coordinator is itself a consensus group C of 2f_C + 1 processes that decides the global outcome.

The protocol proceeds in two consensus rounds:

Round 1 (votes): Each group Pᵢ decides pᵢ's vote vᵢ ∈ {0, 1}.

Round 2 (outcome): The coordinator group C decides the global outcome d ∈ {0, 1}, where d = 1 iff all vᵢ = 1.

Each participant pᵢ observes the outcome decided by C and commits or aborts accordingly.

12.5.2 Protocol

We describe the protocol from the perspective of a single consensus group. Each group Pᵢ runs a standard Paxos instance. The "proposer" for Pᵢ is pᵢ itself (or a designated leader). The value proposed is pᵢ's vote.

Phase 1a (Prepare): Leader of Pᵢ sends PREPARE(n) to acceptors.

Phase 1b (Promise): Acceptors reply PROMISE(n, accepted) where accepted is the highest-numbered accepted proposal.

Phase 2a (Accept): If no acceptor has accepted a value, the leader proposes vᵢ = pᵢ's local vote. Otherwise, it proposes the value already accepted (to preserve agreement).

Phase 2b (Accepted): Acceptors reply ACCEPTED(n, value).

Once a majority of Pᵢ accepts vᵢ, the vote is decided. The coordinator group C observes the decided votes and runs its own Paxos instance to decide d = AND(v₁, v₂, ..., v_N).

Theorem 12.6 (Paxos Commit Non-blocking). Paxos Commit satisfies AC1–AC3 and guarantees that every correct process decides, provided that a majority of each consensus group remains operational.

Proof. AC1 follows from Paxos's agreement property applied to each consensus instance. AC2 follows from the definition of d: d = 1 requires all vᵢ = 1, and vᵢ = 1 is decided only if pᵢ voted yes. AC3 follows from Paxos's termination property: each consensus instance terminates if a majority of its group is operational. ∎

12.5.3 Comparison with 2PC

| Property                   | 2PC                    | Paxos Commit                        |
|----------------------------|------------------------|-------------------------------------|
| Blocking on coordinator    | Yes                    | No (if majority of C operational)   |
| Blocking on participant    | Yes (if pᵢ crashes)    | No (if majority of Pᵢ operational)  |
| Network partitions         | Unsafe (may block)     | Safe (majority side decides)        |
| Message complexity         | O(N) per phase         | O(N · f) per consensus instance     |
| Stable storage per decision | 1 forced write         | 2 forced writes (prepare + accept)  |
| Failure model              | Crash (no partitions)  | Asynchronous crash with majorities  |

Paxos Commit's cost is latency: the two consensus rounds add 2·(Paxos latency) versus 2·(message round-trip) for 2PC. In practice, Paxos Commit is used in systems where availability during failures outweighs latency in the common case.

12.6 Saga-Based Compensation

Sagas [Garcia-Molina and Salem 1987] sidestep atomic commitment by replacing the atomicity requirement with a weaker notion: the transaction's effect is either the sequential composition of all its sub-transactions, or the sequential composition of compensating sub-transactions. Sagas do not require global agreement; they require that each sub-transaction's compensation is semantically correct.

12.6.1 Definition

A saga T = (T₁, T₂, ..., T_n) is a sequence of sub-transactions. Each Tᵢ has a compensating transaction Cᵢ. The saga executes T₁, T₂, ..., T_n in order. If all complete, the saga commits. If Tⱼ fails, the saga executes C_{j-1}, C_{j-2}, ..., C₁ in reverse order and aborts.

Theorem 12.7 (Saga Compensability). A saga T with compensations C₁, ..., C_n is correct if and only if for every state s reachable by executing T₁, ..., T_{j-1}, executing Tⱼ followed by Cⱼ yields a state equivalent to s.

Proof. By induction on j. For j = 1, the claim is that C₁ undoes T₁ from any state s, which is the definition of compensability. Assume the claim for j-1. If Tⱼ fails after T₁, ..., T_{j-1} have committed, the saga executes C_{j-1}, ..., C₁. By the inductive hypothesis, C_{j-1} undoes T_{j-1} from the state after T₁, ..., T_{j-1}, yielding a state equivalent to the state after T₁, ..., T_{j-2}. Repeating, the state after all compensations is equivalent to the initial state. ∎

12.6.2 Worked Example: Travel Booking

Consider booking a flight, a hotel, and a rental car. Each booking is a sub-transaction with a compensation (cancellation).

```go
type Saga struct {
    steps []SagaStep
}

type SagaStep struct {
    Action      func(ctx context.Context) error
    Compensate  func(ctx context.Context) error
}

func (s *Saga) Run(ctx context.Context) error {
    completed := make([]SagaStep, 0, len(s.steps))

    for _, step := range s.steps {
        if err := step.Action(ctx); err != nil {
            // Compensate in reverse order
            for i := len(completed) - 1; i >= 0; i-- {
                if compErr := completed[i].Compensate(ctx); compErr != nil {
                    // Log and retry; compensation failure is serious
                    log.Printf("compensation failed: %v", compErr)
                }
            }
            return err
        }
        completed = append(completed, step)
    }
    return nil
}
```

12.6.3 Compensability vs. Isolation

Sagas sacrifice isolation: intermediate states are visible to other transactions. In the travel example, after booking the flight but before booking the hotel, the flight reservation is visible. Other transactions may observe this intermediate state. This is acceptable when:

Intermediate states are semantically meaningful (a flight reservation is a valid business state).

Compensations are feasible (cancelling a flight is possible; cancelling a wire transfer is not).

Latency is acceptable (sagas may run for minutes or days).

Compensations must be idempotent and retryable: if cancelFlight fails due to a transient error, the saga coordinator must retry. Compensations must also be commutative with other transactions' effects to the extent that the business logic permits.

12.6.4 Saga Coordinators

In practice, saga coordination is centralized in a coordinator (or orchestrator) that tracks the saga's state and drives execution. Two styles exist:

Orchestration: A central coordinator invokes each step and handles compensation. The coordinator's state must be durable (persisted to a database) to survive coordinator crashes.

Choreography: Each step publishes events; subsequent steps subscribe to events and execute. No central coordinator exists, but the logic is distributed and harder to reason about.

Orchestration is preferred when the saga's logic is complex or when compensations require coordination. Choreography is preferred when steps are loosely coupled and the logic is simple.

12.7 Comparing the Approaches

We now compare 2PC, 3PC, Paxos Commit, and sagas across several dimensions.

12.7.1 Safety and Liveness

| Protocol      | Agreement   | Termination (crash)   | Termination (partition)   |
|---------------|-------------|-----------------------|---------------------------|
| 2PC           | Yes         | Blocking              | Blocking                  |
| 3PC           | Yes (no partition) | Yes            | Unsafe                    |
| Paxos Commit  | Yes         | Yes (majority)        | Yes (majority side)       |
| Saga          | N/A (no global agreement) | Yes | Yes |

2PC provides agreement but may block indefinitely. 3PC provides termination under crash failures but is unsafe under partitions. Paxos Commit provides both, at the cost of additional consensus rounds. Sagas avoid the problem by not requiring global agreement.

12.7.2 Latency

2PC requires 2 message rounds plus 2 forced log writes (prepare, commit). 3PC requires 3 rounds plus 3 writes. Paxos Commit requires 2 consensus rounds (each with 2 phases) plus 2 writes per participant. Sagas require n sequential sub-transactions but no global coordination.

In a LAN with 0.5 ms round-trip and 10 ms disk flush:

| Protocol      | Latency (happy path)   |
|---------------|------------------------|
| 2PC           | ~22 ms                 |
| 3PC           | ~33 ms                 |
| Paxos Commit  | ~25 ms                 |
| Saga (n = 3)  | ~60 ms (sequential)    |

Sagas are slower for short transactions but scale better for long-running business processes.

12.7.3 Applicability

2PC is appropriate when:

All participants are trusted and cooperative.

Blocking is acceptable (short transactions, low failure rate).

Latency must be minimal.

3PC is appropriate when:

The network is reliable (no partitions).

Termination under coordinator crash is essential.

The additional round of communication is acceptable.

Paxos Commit is appropriate when:

Availability during failures is critical.

Participants can tolerate the latency of consensus.

The system is already replicated.

Sagas are appropriate when:

Compensations are semantically meaningful.

Isolation can be relaxed.

Transactions span organizational boundaries.

Transactions are long-running.

12.7.4 Isolation Anomalies in Sagas

Because sagas release locks after each sub-transaction, they are vulnerable to anomalies that 2PC prevents:

Lost update: Two sagas read the same value, compute updates, and write. The second write overwrites the first.

Dirty read: A saga reads a value written by another saga's sub-transaction that is later compensated.

Non-repeatable read: A saga reads a value twice and gets different results because another saga's sub-transaction committed in between.

Mitigations include semantic locks (application-level flags that indicate a compensation is possible), commutative operations (design sub-transactions so their effects commute), and optimistic concurrency (detect conflicts at saga completion and compensate).

Distributed Transactions

Distributed transactions are transactions that span multiple nodes in a distributed system. They are a fundamental concept in distributed systems, as they allow for the coordination of operations across multiple nodes, ensuring that either all operations are completed, or none are. This is known as atomicity.

In this chapter, we will explore the algorithms and techniques used to implement distributed transactions, including two-phase commit (2PC) and three-phase commit (3PC). We will also discuss the challenges of implementing distributed transactions, such as handling failures and ensuring consistency.

The Need for Distributed Transactions

Consider a simple banking application, where a user wants to transfer $100 from account A to account B. If both accounts are on the same node, this can be implemented as a simple transaction:

```
BEGIN TRANSACTION;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE account_id = 'A';
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 100 WHERE account_id = 'B';
COMMIT;
```

However, if account A is on node 1 and account B is on node 2, this simple transaction will not work. The two updates must be coordinated across the two nodes, ensuring that either both updates are completed, or neither are. This is where distributed transactions come in.

Two-Phase Commit (2PC)

Two-phase commit is a protocol for implementing distributed transactions. It is a blocking protocol, meaning that nodes can be left waiting for a response from the coordinator. 2PC involves two phases:

Prepare Phase: The coordinator sends a "prepare" message to all participants, asking them to prepare to commit the transaction. If a participant is able to prepare, it responds with a "yes" message, indicating that it is ready to commit. If a participant is unable to prepare, it responds with a "no" message, indicating that it is unable to commit.

Commit Phase: If the coordinator receives "yes" messages from all participants, it sends a "commit" message to all participants, instructing them to commit the transaction. If the coordinator receives any "no" messages, it sends an "abort" message to all participants, instructing them to abort the transaction.

Let's implement 2PC in Python. We'll use a simple message-passing model, where the coordinator and participants communicate by sending messages.

        # Phase 1: Prepare
        responses = []
        for participant in self.participants:
            response = participant.prepare(transaction)
            responses.append(response)
            if response == 'no':

        if all(response == 'yes' for response in responses):

        else:

Handling Failures in 2PC

One of the biggest challenges with 2PC is handling failures. If the coordinator fails after sending the "prepare" messages but before sending the "commit" or "abort" messages, the participants will be left in a "prepared" state, waiting for a response. This is known as the "in-doubt" state.

To handle this, participants can use a timeout. If a participant doesn't receive a response from the coordinator within a certain time, it can assume that the coordinator has failed and can abort the transaction. However, this can lead to inconsistencies, as some participants may have committed the transaction before the timeout, while others may have aborted it.

Another approach is to use a "coordinator log", where the coordinator writes its decision to a log before sending the messages to the participants. If the coordinator fails, a new coordinator can be elected and can use the log to determine the outcome of the transaction.

Three-Phase Commit (3PC)

Three-phase commit is an extension of 2PC that attempts to address some of its limitations. 3PC involves three phases:

CanCommit Phase: The coordinator sends a "canCommit" message to all participants, asking them if they can commit the transaction. If a participant can commit, it responds with a "yes" message. If it cannot, it responds with a "no" message.

PreCommit Phase: If the coordinator receives "yes" messages from all participants, it sends a "preCommit" message to all participants, instructing them to prepare to commit. If a participant is able to prepare, it responds with an "ack" message.

DoCommit Phase: If the coordinator receives "ack" messages from all participants, it sends a "doCommit" message to all participants, instructing them to commit the transaction.

The key idea behind 3PC is to add an extra phase, which allows the coordinator to inform the participants of its decision before they actually commit. This reduces the window of time during which the participants are in the "in-doubt" state.

While 3PC attempts to address some of the limitations of 2PC, it introduces its own challenges. For example, 3PC requires more communication between the coordinator and participants, which can increase latency. Additionally, 3PC is still vulnerable to certain types of failures, such as network partitions.

In practice, 2PC is more commonly used than 3PC, as it is simpler and has been proven to work well in practice. However, 3PC is still an important concept to understand, as it illustrates the trade-offs involved in designing distributed algorithms.

## 1. Introduction to Distributed Transactions

### 1.1 The Problem Space

Consider a banking system where a customer wants to transfer $500 from an account held at Bank A to an account held at Bank B. This operation involves:

1. Debiting $500 from the account at Bank A
2. Crediting $500 to the account at Bank B

If the debit succeeds but the credit fails, $500 has vanished. If the credit succeeds but the debit fails, $500 has been created from nothing. Neither outcome is acceptable.

In a centralized system, this is solved with a simple transaction:

```sql
BEGIN TRANSACTION;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 500 WHERE account_id = 'source';
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 500 WHERE account_id = 'dest';
COMMIT;
```

The database engine ensures atomicity through its transaction log. But when the two accounts live on different machines, we need something more sophisticated.

### 1.2 ACID Properties in a Distributed Context

The ACID properties take on new meaning when distributed:

**Atomicity**: Either all nodes commit their portion of the transaction, or none do. This is the hardest property to guarantee across machines.

**Consistency**: The system must move from one consistent state to another, even when the intermediate states span multiple machines.

**Isolation**: Concurrent transactions must not observe each other's partial states, even when those states span multiple machines.

**Durability**: Once a transaction commits, it must remain committed even if some nodes fail.

### 1.3 System Model

Before diving into algorithms, we must establish our system model. We assume:

- **Nodes**: Independent computers that can fail independently
- **Network**: Messages can be delayed, lost, duplicated, or reordered
- **Crash failures**: Nodes can crash and recover, but do not act maliciously (Byzantine failures are out of scope)
- **Stable storage**: Nodes have persistent storage that survives crashes

The fundamental impossibility result we must contend with is the **Two Generals Problem**: it is impossible to guarantee atomic commit in the presence of both node failures and network failures. Every distributed commit protocol must make trade-offs.

### 1.4 The Blocking vs. Non-Blocking Distinction

A commit protocol is **blocking** if a failure can force participants to wait indefinitely for a decision. It is **non-blocking** if participants can always eventually determine the outcome.

2PC is blocking. 3PC attempts to be non-blocking but has its own issues. Both are explored in this chapter.

## 2. Two-Phase Commit (2PC)

### 2.1 Protocol Overview

Two-Phase Commit is the classic atomic commit protocol, first described by Gray in 1978. It involves a single **coordinator** and multiple **participants** (also called cohorts or workers).

The protocol proceeds in two phases:

**Phase 1: Prepare (Voting) Phase**
1. The coordinator sends a `PREPARE` message to all participants
2. Each participant processes the transaction up to the point of commit
3. Each participant writes an "intent to commit" record to stable storage
4. Each participant responds with either `VOTE_COMMIT` or `VOTE_ABORT`

**Phase 2: Commit/Abort Phase**
1. If the coordinator receives `VOTE_COMMIT` from all participants:
   - The coordinator writes a "commit" record to stable storage
   - The coordinator sends `COMMIT` to all participants
   - Participants commit and acknowledge
2. If any participant votes `VOTE_ABORT` (or times out):
   - The coordinator writes an "abort" record to stable storage
   - The coordinator sends `ABORT` to all participants
   - Participants abort and acknowledge

### 2.4 The Write-Ahead Log

Critical to 2PC is the write-ahead log (WAL). Each node maintains a log that records the transaction's state transitions. The log must be written to stable storage *before* the corresponding action is taken.

The log records include:

- **PREPARED**: Participant has locked resources and is ready to commit
- **VOTE_COMMIT**: Participant's vote (implicit in PREPARED)
- **COMMIT**: Coordinator's decision to commit
- **ABORT**: Coordinator's decision to abort
- **COMMITTED**: Participant has committed locally
- **ABORTED**: Participant has aborted locally
- **DONE**: Transaction is fully complete

### 2.5 Failure Scenarios

#### 2.5.1 Participant Fails Before Voting

If participant P fails before responding to PREPARE, the coordinator will not receive P's vote. The coordinator can safely abort the transaction because P has not yet acquired any resources that would block other transactions.

**Recovery**: Coordinator aborts. When P recovers, it finds no PREPARED record in its log and knows the transaction was aborted.

#### 2.5.2 Participant Fails After Voting Commit

If participant P votes COMMIT but fails before receiving the coordinator's decision, P is in the "in-doubt" state. P has acquired locks and written a PREPARED record, but doesn't know whether to commit or abort.

**Recovery**: When P recovers, it reads its log and finds the PREPARED record. It must ask the coordinator for the decision. This is the **blocking** problem of 2PC: if the coordinator has also failed, P must wait until the coordinator recovers.

#### 2.5.3 Coordinator Fails Before Sending Decision

If the coordinator fails after receiving all votes but before sending the decision, all participants are in the in-doubt state.

**Recovery**: When the coordinator recovers, it reads its log to determine the decision and re-sends it to all participants. Participants must wait for the coordinator to recover.

#### 2.5.4 Coordinator Fails After Sending Decision to Some Participants

If the coordinator sends COMMIT to participants A and B but fails before sending to C, we have an inconsistency risk. A and B may commit while C is still in-doubt.

**Recovery**: The coordinator's log contains the COMMIT record. Upon recovery, the coordinator re-sends the decision to all participants. C will eventually receive the COMMIT and commit.

#### 2.5.5 Network Partition

If the network partitions the coordinator from some participants, those participants are effectively in the in-doubt state until the partition heals.

This is where 2PC's blocking nature is most problematic. A partition that lasts hours will block transactions for hours.

### 2.6 Timeout Handling

Timeouts are essential for liveness. The protocol uses two types:

**Coordinator Timeout**: If the coordinator doesn't receive all votes within a timeout period, it aborts the transaction. This is safe because a participant that hasn't voted has not yet acquired resources.

**Participant Timeout**: If a participant is in the in-doubt state and doesn't receive the coordinator's decision within a timeout period, it can query the coordinator. In basic 2PC, the participant cannot unilaterally decide to abort because the coordinator might have decided to commit.

class WriteAheadLog:
    """
    Write-ahead log for transaction state.
    
    In a production system, this would use fsync() to ensure
    durability. For this implementation, we use a simple file
    with explicit flush.
    """
    
    def __init__(self, node_id: str, log_dir: str = "/tmp/2pc_logs"):
        self.node_id = node_id
        self.log_dir = log_dir
        self.log_file = os.path.join(log_dir, f"{node_id}.wal")
        self._lock = threading.Lock()
        
        os.makedirs(log_dir, exist_ok=True)
    
    def append(self, record: Dict) -> None:
        """Append a record to the log and force it to stable storage."""
        with self._lock:
            record['timestamp'] = time.time()
            record['node_id'] = self.node_id
            
            with open(self.log_file, 'ab') as f:
                f.write(pickle.dumps(record))
                f.flush()
                os.fsync(f.fileno())
    
    def read_all(self) -> List[Dict]:
        """Read all records from the log."""
        records = []
        if not os.path.exists(self.log_file):
            return records
        
        with open(self.log_file, 'rb') as f:
            while True:
                try:
                    record = pickle.load(f)
                    records.append(record)
                except EOFError:
                    break
        
        return records
    
    def get_latest_state(self, txn_id: str) -> Optional[Dict]:
        """Get the latest log record for a transaction."""
        records = [r for r in self.read_all() if r.get('txn_id') == txn_id]
        return records[-1] if records else None

    """
    A participant in the 2PC protocol.
    
    The participant manages local transaction state and responds

                 vote_timeout: float = 5.0):
        self.node_id = node_id
        self.host = host
        self.port = port
        self.coordinator_addr = (coordinator_host, coordinator_port)
        self.vote_timeout = vote_timeout
        
        self.logger = logging.getLogger(f"Participant-{node_id}")
        self.wal = WriteAheadLog(node_id)
        
        # Transaction state: txn_id -> state
        self.transactions: Dict[str, TransactionState] = {}
        
        # Lock for state transitions
        self._lock = threading.Lock()
        
        # Server socket for receiving messages
        self._server_socket = None
        self._running = False
        
        # Callback for applying transactions
        self.apply_callback = None
        self.abort_callback = None
    
    def start(self) -> None:
        """Start the participant's message server."""
        self._server_socket = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM)
        self._server_socket.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
        self._server_socket.bind((self.host, self.port))
        self._server_socket.listen(10)
        
        self._running = True
        
        # Start message handling thread
        thread = threading.Thread(target=self._message_loop, daemon=True)
        thread.start()
        
        self.logger.info(f"Participant started on {self.host}:{self.port}")
    
    def stop(self) -> None:
        """Stop the participant."""
        self._running = False
        if self._server_socket:
            self._server_socket.close()
    
    def _message_loop(self) -> None:
        """Main message handling loop."""
        while self._running:
            try:
                client_socket, addr = self._server_socket.accept()
                thread = threading.Thread(
                    target=self._handle_connection,
                    args=(client_socket, addr),
                    daemon=True
                )
                thread.start()
            except OSError:
                break
    
    def _handle_connection(self, sock: socket.socket, addr) -> None:
        """Handle a single connection."""
        try:
            data = sock.recv(65536).decode('utf-8')
            if data:
                message = Message.from_json(data)
                response = self._process_message(message)
                if response:
                    sock.send(response.to_json().encode('utf-8'))
        except Exception as e:
            self.logger.error(f"Error handling connection: {e}")
        finally:
            sock.close()
    
    def _process_message(self, message: Message) -> Optional[Message]:
        """Process an incoming message and return a response."""
        self.logger.debug(f"Received {message.msg_type.value} for txn {message.txn_id}")
        
        if message.msg_type == MessageType.PREPARE:
            return self._handle_prepare(message)
        elif message.msg_type == MessageType.COMMIT:
            return self._handle_commit(message)
        elif message.msg_type == MessageType.ABORT:
            return self._handle_abort(message)
        elif message.msg_type == MessageType.QUERY_STATUS:
            return self._handle_query(message)
        
        return None
    
    def _handle_prepare(self, message: Message) -> Message:
        """Handle PREPARE message from coordinator."""
        txn_id = message.txn_id
        
        with self._lock:
            # Check if we already have state for this transaction
            current_state = self.transactions.get(txn_id)
            
            if current_state == TransactionState.PREPARED:
                # Already prepared, just confirm
                self.logger.debug(f"Already prepared for txn {txn_id}")
                return Message(
                    msg_type=MessageType.VOTE_COMMIT,
                    txn_id=txn_id,
                    sender=self.node_id
                )
            
            if current_state in (TransactionState.COMMITTED, TransactionState.ABORTED):
                # Transaction already completed
                self.logger.warning(f"Received PREPARE for completed txn {txn_id}")
                return Message(
                    msg_type=MessageType.VOTE_ABORT,
                    txn_id=txn_id,
                    sender=self.node_id
                )
            
            # Attempt to prepare the transaction
            # This involves:
            # 1. Acquiring necessary locks
            # 2. Writing undo/redo records to local log
            # 3. Writing PREPARED record to WAL
            
            try:
                # Write PREPARED record to WAL
                self.wal.append({
                    'txn_id': txn_id,
                    'state': TransactionState.PREPARED.value,
                    'payload': message.payload
                })
                
                self.transactions[txn_id] = TransactionState.PREPARED
                
                self.logger.info(f"Prepared for txn {txn_id}")
                
                return Message(
                    msg_type=MessageType.VOTE_COMMIT,
                    txn_id=txn_id,
                    sender=self.node_id
                )
            
            except Exception as e:
                self.logger.error(f"Failed to prepare for txn {txn_id}: {e}")
                
                # Write ABORT record to WAL
                self.wal.append({
                    'txn_id': txn_id,
                    'state': TransactionState.ABORTED.value
                })
                
                self.transactions[txn_id] = TransactionState.ABORTED
                
                return Message(
                    msg_type=MessageType.VOTE_ABORT,
                    txn_id=txn_id,
                    sender=self.node_id
                )
    
    def _handle_commit(self, message: Message) -> Message:
        """Handle COMMIT decision from coordinator."""
        txn_id = message.txn_id
        
        with self._lock:
            current_state = self.transactions.get(txn_id)
            
            if current_state == TransactionState.PREPARED:
                # Apply the transaction locally
                if self.apply_callback:
                    self.apply_callback(txn_id, message.payload)
                
                # Write COMMITTED record to WAL
                self.wal.append({
                    'txn_id': txn_id,
                    'state': TransactionState.COMMITTED.value
                })
                
                self.transactions[txn_id] = TransactionState.COMMITTED
                
                self.logger.info(f"Committed txn {txn_id}")
            
            elif current_state == TransactionState.COMMITTED:
                # Already committed (duplicate message)
                self.logger.debug(f"Already committed txn {txn_id}")
            
            elif current_state is None:
                self.logger.warning(f"Received COMMIT for unknown txn {txn_id}")
                # This shouldn't happen in normal operation
                # It could indicate a crash between prepare and commit
            
            elif current_state == TransactionState.ABORTED:
                self.logger.error(f"Received COMMIT for aborted txn {txn_id}")
                # This is a protocol violation
            
            return Message(
                msg_type=MessageType.ACK,
                txn_id=txn_id,
                sender=self.node_id
            )
    
    def _handle_abort(self, message: Message) -> Message:
        """Handle ABORT decision from coordinator."""
        txn_id = message.txn_id
        
        with self._lock:
            current_state = self.transactions.get(txn_id)
            
            if current_state == TransactionState.PREPARED:
                # Rollback local changes
                if self.abort_callback:
                    self.abort_callback(txn_id, message.payload)
                
                # Write ABORTED record to WAL
                self.wal.append({
                    'txn_id': txn_id,
                    'state': TransactionState.ABORTED.value
                })
                
                self.transactions[txn_id] = TransactionState.ABORTED
                
                self.logger.info(f"Aborted txn {txn_id}")
            
            elif current_state == TransactionState.ABORTED:
                # Already aborted
                self.logger.debug(f"Already aborted txn {txn_id}")
            
            return Message(
                msg_type=MessageType.ACK,
                txn_id=txn_id,
                sender=self.node_id
            )
    
    def _handle_query(self, message: Message) -> Message:
        """Handle status query from recovering coordinator."""
        txn_id = message.txn_id
        
        with self._lock:
            state = self.transactions.get(txn_id)
            
            if state == TransactionState.COMMITTED:
                msg_type = MessageType.STATUS_COMMITTED
            elif state == TransactionState.ABORTED:
                msg_type = MessageType.STATUS_ABORTED
            elif state == TransactionState.PREPARED:
                msg_type = MessageType.STATUS_PREPARED
            else:
                msg_type = MessageType.STATUS_UNKNOWN
            
            return Message(
                msg_type=msg_type,
                txn_id=txn_id,
                sender=self.node_id
            )
    
    def recover(self) -> None:
        """
        Recovery procedure after a crash.
        
        Reads the WAL and determines the state of each transaction.
        For in-doubt transactions (PREPARED but no decision), queries
        the coordinator.
        """
        self.logger.info("Starting recovery...")
        
        records = self.wal.read_all()
        
        # Group records by transaction
        txn_records: Dict[str, List[Dict]] = {}
        for record in records:
            txn_id = record.get('txn_id')
            if txn_id:
                txn_records.setdefault(txn_id, []).append(record)
        
        for txn_id, txn_log in txn_records.items():
            latest = txn_log[-1]
            state = latest.get('state')
            
            if state == TransactionState.PREPARED.value:
                # In-doubt transaction - must query coordinator
                self.logger.warning(f"In-doubt transaction {txn_id}, querying coordinator")
                decision = self._query_coordinator(txn_id)
                
                if decision == 'COMMIT':
                    self.transactions[txn_id] = TransactionState.COMMITTED
                    self.wal.append({'txn_id': txn_id, 'state': 'COMMITTED'})
                elif decision == 'ABORT':
                    self.transactions[txn_id] = TransactionState.ABORTED
                    self.wal.append({'txn_id': txn_id, 'state': 'ABORTED'})
                else:
                    # Coordinator doesn't know - safe to abort
                    self.logger.info(f"Coordinator unknown for {txn_id}, aborting")
                    self.transactions[txn_id] = TransactionState.ABORTED
                    self.wal.append({'txn_id': txn_id, 'state': 'ABORTED'})
            
            elif state == TransactionState.COMMITTED.value:
                self.transactions[txn_id] = TransactionState.COMMITTED
            
            elif state == TransactionState.ABORTED.value:
                self.transactions[txn_id] = TransactionState.ABORTED
        
        self.logger.info(f"Recovery complete. {len(self.transactions)} transactions recovered.")

        try:

            sock.settimeout(self.vote_timeout)

                msg_type=MessageType.QUERY_STATUS,
                txn_id=txn_id,
                sender=self.node_id
            )
            sock.send(query.to_json().encode('utf-8'))
            
            response_data = sock.recv(65536).decode('utf-8')
            response = Message.from_json(response_data)
            
            sock.close()
            
            if response.msg_type == MessageType.STATUS_COMMITTED:
                return 'COMMIT'
            elif response.msg_type == MessageType.STATUS_ABORTED:
                return 'ABORT'
            
        except Exception as e:
            self.logger.error(f"Failed to query coordinator: {e}")
        
        return None

Distributed Transactions

Distributed transactions are transactions that span multiple nodes in a distributed system. They are a fundamental concept in distributed systems, as they allow for the coordination of operations across multiple nodes, ensuring that either all operations are completed, or none are. This is known as atomicity.

In this chapter, we will explore the algorithms and techniques used to implement distributed transactions, including two-phase commit (2PC) and three-phase commit (3PC). We will also discuss the challenges of implementing distributed transactions, such as handling failures and ensuring consistency.

The Need for Distributed Transactions

Consider a simple banking application, where a user wants to transfer $100 from account A to account B. If both accounts are on the same node, this is a simple operation. However, if account A is on node 1 and account B is on node 2, the operation becomes more complex. We need to ensure that either both the debit from account A and the credit to account B are completed, or neither are. If we debit account A but fail to credit account B, we have lost $100. If we credit account B but fail to debit account A, we have created $100 out of thin air.

This is where distributed transactions come in. They allow us to coordinate the operations on multiple nodes, ensuring that either all operations are completed, or none are.

Two-Phase Commit (2PC)

Two-phase commit is a widely used algorithm for implementing distributed transactions. It is a blocking algorithm, meaning that if a node fails during the commit process, the transaction may be left in an inconsistent state until the node recovers.

The algorithm consists of two phases:

Phase 1: Prepare Phase

The coordinator sends a prepare message to all participants.

Each participant checks if it can commit the transaction. If it can, it writes a "prepared" record to its log and sends an "agree" message to the coordinator. If it cannot, it sends an "abort" message.

Phase 2: Commit Phase

If the coordinator receives "agree" from all participants, it sends a "commit" message to all participants. Otherwise, it sends an "abort" message.

Each participant, upon receiving a "commit" message, writes a "commit" record to its log and completes the transaction. Upon receiving an "abort" message, it writes an "abort" record to its log and aborts the transaction.

Challenges with 2PC

Blocking: If the coordinator fails after sending "prepare" but before sending "commit" or "abort", participants are blocked waiting for a decision. They cannot unilaterally decide to commit or abort, as this could lead to inconsistency.

In-doubt transactions: Transactions that have received "prepare" but not yet "commit" or "abort" are called in-doubt transactions. These transactions hold locks on resources, potentially blocking other transactions.

Single point of failure: The coordinator is a single point of failure. If it fails, the entire system may be blocked.

Three-Phase Commit (3PC)

Three-phase commit is an extension of 2PC that addresses some of its limitations. It adds an additional phase, called the "pre-commit" phase, which reduces the blocking window.

The algorithm consists of three phases:

Phase 1: Prepare Phase (CanCommit)

The coordinator sends a canCommit message to all participants.

Each participant checks if it can commit the transaction. If it can, it writes a "prepared" record to its log and sends a "yes" vote to the coordinator. If it cannot, it sends a "no" vote.

Phase 2: Pre-Commit Phase

If the coordinator receives "yes" from all participants, it sends a preCommit message to all participants. Otherwise, it sends an "abort" message.

Each participant, upon receiving a preCommit message, writes a "pre-commit" record to its log and sends an "ack" message to the coordinator.

Phase 3: Commit Phase (DoCommit)

If the coordinator receives "ack" from all participants, it sends a doCommit message to all participants.

Each participant, upon receiving a doCommit message, writes a "commit" record to its log and completes the transaction.
